Ariel will investigatethe atmospheres of many hundreds of diverse planets orbiting different types of stars to address fundamental scientific questions.Ariel is designed as a dedicated survey mission for transit and eclipse spectroscopy. Ariel observations require a specifically designed, stable payload and satellite platform with broad, instantaneous wavelength coverage extending from the visible to the infra-red (500 nm to 7.8 m). The detector technology selected to cover this wave range makes use of HgCdTe CMOS detectors. These detectors are optimised for astronomical observations, providing high Quantum Efficiency with low noise. As the cut-off wavelength of these detectors increase, these performance characteristic require operations in a colder environment. While the Ariel FGS instrument (500 nm to 1.95 m) can operate by making use of the passive cooling capabilities of the Ariel PLM (with the V-groove radiators), the AIRSinstrument (1.95 m to 7.8 m) requires further cooling down to 42 K with an active cryo-cooler. A Joule-Thomson (JT) cooler is therefore integrated in the system design and makes use of Neon as its working fluid (boiling point of 27.05 K at 1 atm). This cooler is developed by RAL (UK), under the responsibility of the UK Space Agency, within the AMC, as specified in the MLA, and builds on their experience from the Planck Helium JT cooler. This Ne JT Cooler is controlled by a warm electronic box, the CCE (Cooler Control Electronics), which is the subject of this procurement. While the cooler remains under the AMC's responsibility through UKSA and RAL(UK), the Agency, through the Ariel Project, has agreed to provide support to UKSA for the procurement of the CCE. Through this activity, the Contractor will be requested to provide the CCE, including development models as well as the Flight Model and spares.
